paragraphs.heading: What it does
paragraphs.text: The multinomial theorem tells you how to expand a power of a sum, writing the answer using powers of each term of the sum. It takes the binomial theorem, which works for binomials, and extends it to multinomials. When the sum has just two terms, that is the case m = 2, the multinomial theorem shrinks back to the binomial theorem it grew out of.

paragraphs.heading: The shape of the expansion
paragraphs.text: The expansion is a big sum. It runs over every possible choice of nonnegative whole-number indices k₁ through kₘ whose total is n. Put another way, in every term of the expansion, the exponents on the xᵢ have to add up to n. So the power n of the whole sum is shared out among the terms in each piece of the answer.

paragraphs.heading: What the coefficients count
paragraphs.text: The numbers in front of each term, the multinomial coefficients, have a direct meaning in counting. Each one is the number of ways to drop n distinct objects into m distinct bins so that the first bin gets k₁ objects, the second gets k₂, and so on. In statistical mechanics and in combinatorics, these coefficients come straight out of binomial coefficients whenever items carry a spread of labels. From N items, first choose n₁ of them to get label 1. Then from the N − n₁ left, choose n₂ to get label 2, and from the N − n₁ − n₂ still left, choose n₃ to get label 3.

paragraphs.heading: Proof and patterns
paragraphs.text: One proof uses the binomial theorem together with induction on m, the number of indices. To find the largest power of a prime p dividing a multinomial coefficient, you can use a generalization of Kummer's theorem. The theorem also lets you extend Pascal's triangle, or Pascal's pyramid, to a shape called Pascal's simplex. That gives a quick way to build a lookup table of multinomial coefficients.
